title: Alpha diversity and rarefaction
text: Alpha diversity diversity within one sample site. Counting species obvious measure, count depends hard looked: second day sampling always adds species. Two ideas solve : Hill numbers put richness, Shannon Simpson diversity one scale, effective number species: number equally common species give diversity. order q sets much rare species count (q = 0 equally, q = 1 proportion frequency, q = 2 mostly common ones). Sample coverage estimated proportion community’s individuals (occurrences) belong species already sample. estimated singletons (f1, species seen ) doubletons (f2): many singletons mean many species still unseen. Comparing sites equal coverage compares equal completeness, fairer comparing equal sample size (Chao Jost 2012). examples use png_ants: ants recorded nutrient baits along Mt Wilhelm elevational gradient Papua New Guinea, dry wet seasons (Moses et al. 2023). bait species found counts one occurrence.

title: Alpha diversity and rarefaction
text: Hill numbers express diversity effective number species. Order q = 0 richness, q = 1 weights species frequency q = 2 emphasises dominant species. read . n number occurrences, diversity observed Hill number. Diversity always falls q = 0 q = 2; steeper fall, uneven community (species dominate). 200 m dry season, 16 species equivalent 12.3 equally common ones (q = 1) 9.9 dominant ones (q = 2): fairly even community.

title: Partitioning beta diversity
text: Two communities can differ two ways: Sørensen dissimilarity (0 = species, 1 = species shared) mixes . Baselga’s partition splits turnover (Simpson dissimilarity) nestedness, add total, can say sites differ, much. Conservation advice differs: turnover every site needed protect species; nestedness richest site protects .

title: Partitioning beta diversity
text: Turnover nestedness add total. Use index = "jaccard" Jaccard family. results match betapart package. read . Sites differ strongly (mean total dissimilarity 0.86-0.87: average pair shares 13% species), almost difference turnover (0.82-0.83) rather nestedness (0.04). Ant species replaced along Mt Wilhelm, simply lost. Several high-elevation pairs share species (total = 1).

title: Partitioning beta diversity
text: beta_decay() adds distance sites along gradient. turnover rises elevational distance nestedness stays low.  beta_decay_model() fits distance-decay curve similarities (one minus dissimilarity) tests . exponential model S = exp(-b d) gives similarity sites elevation rate b; half_distance elevational distance similarity halves. Pairs sites share sites, independent: p-value comes permuting site labels, Mantel test, refitting model time. read . wet season similarity decays steeply elevational distance: halves every 293 m, curve explains 69% variation among pairs (pseudo_r2), permutation test significant (P = 0.017). dry season curve flat significant (P = 0.35): sites near already dissimilar (= 0.26, similarity zero distance), sparse dry-season samples share species chance. five sites per season 120 distinct permutations, smallest attainable p-value near 0.01 however strong pattern.

title: An elevational-gradient workflow
text: Richness count, model Poisson GLM; quadratic term tests mid-elevation peak. #> ── What the data show ── #>  #> • Sites: "20" #> • Species: "30" #> • Data: "abundances" #> • Zeros: "67%" — many zeros: shared absences must not make sites similar #>   (Hellinger or Bray-Curtis) #> • Species in one site only: "10%" #> • Gradient length (DCA axis 1, SD units): "3.52" — intermediate: linear or #>   unimodal methods both suit #> • Site variables (model terms): "7" — many terms for the sites: select #>   variables (forward selection) #>  #> ── Recommended ── #>  #> Approach: Constrained (direct, canonical) ordination #> You have a hypothesis that measured site variables explain composition. #> Method: RDA on Hellinger-transformed data (or db-RDA) #> Gradient length 3.5 SD. #> ord <- ord_fit(data, abundance = abundance, method = "rda", transform = "hellinger", formula = ~A1 + Moisture + Management) #> Select: Forward selection of variables #> Too many or collinear variables inflate the explained variation and make the #> test unreliable. #> ord_select(data, abundance = abundance, formula = ~A1 + Moisture + Management) #> Test: Permutation tests: the whole model, each axis and each term #> The F-test of a constrained ordination has no parametric distribution; #> permuting sites gives p-values. #> ord_test(ord, by = "model"); ord_test(ord, by = "axis"); ord_test(ord, by = "margin") #> Plots: Triplot; species response curves along the main variable; t-value biplot #> or Van Dobben circles #> The triplot shows sites, species and variables together; response curves show #> each species' optimum and tolerance with confidence bands; Van Dobben circles #> single out the species that respond significantly. #> autoplot(ord) #> autoplot(ord, type = "response", variable = "<numeric>") #> autoplot(ord, type = "vandobben", variable = "<numeric>") #> Interpret: Plain-language explanation of the tables and the diagram #> Variation explained, tests, directions of variables, groups, species at each #> end of the axes, and how to read the plot. #> ord_interpret(ord) rda_dune <- ord_fit(dune_l,   abundance = abundance, method = "rda", transform = "hellinger",   formula = ~ A1 + Moisture + Management ) tidyvisor(rda_dune, permutations = 199) #>  #> ── tidyvisor: what the results show ──────────────────────────────────────────── #>  #> ── Overview ── #>  #> • A redundancy analysis (RDA) of 20 sites and 30 species #>   (Hellinger-transformed), constrained by A1, Moisture, Management. #>  #> ── Variation ── #>  #> • The site variables explain 58.1% of the variation in composition (adjusted R² #>   = 33.7%, allowing for the number of variables). #> • The first two constrained axes hold 26.9% and 16.1% of the total variation #>   (73.9% of the explained part). #>  #> ── Tests ── #>  #> • Overall, composition is significantly related to the site variables #>   (permutation F = 2.38, p = 0.005, 199 permutations). #> • A1 has no significant unique effect (F = 1.28, p = 0.23), after allowing for #>   the other variables. #> • Moisture has a significant unique effect (F = 1.87, p = 0.01), after allowing #>   for the other variables. #> • Management has a significant unique effect (F = 1.87, p = 0.02), after #>   allowing for the other variables. #>  #> ── Site variables ── #>  #> • A1 increases towards the left of the diagram, mostly along the first axis #>   (biplot scores -0.63, -0.10). #> • Moisture L increases towards the left of the diagram, mostly along the first #>   axis (biplot scores -0.96, 0.03). #> • Moisture Q increases towards the lower left of the diagram, mostly along the #>   second axis (biplot scores -0.16, -0.32). #> • Moisture C increases towards the lower left of the diagram, mostly along the #>   second axis (biplot scores -0.17, -0.23). #> • Moisture: 1 lies towards the right; 2 lies towards the right; 4 lies towards #>   the top; 5 lies towards the left. The further apart two centroids, the more #>   the composition of their sites differs. #> • Management: BF lies towards the right; HF lies towards the upper right; NM #>   lies towards the lower left; SF lies towards the top. The further apart two #>   centroids, the more the composition of their sites differs. #>  #> ── Species ── #>  #> • Axis 1 (RDA1) runs from Agrostol, Eleopalu, Ranuflam (negative end) to #>   Lolipere, Poaprat, Planlanc (positive end). #> • Axis 2 (RDA2) runs from Salirepe, Scorautu, Anthodor (negative end) to #>   Poatriv, Alopgeni, Agrostol (positive end). #>  #> ── Reading the diagram ── #>  #> • Sites (circles) close together have similar species composition. #> • With species scaling, the angles between species (and between species and #>   variable arrows) approximate their correlations; distances between sites are #>   only approximate. #> • Project a site or species perpendicularly onto an arrow: the further along #>   the arrow, the higher the variable (or the stronger the species' association #>   with it). #> • Triangles are the centroids of the factor levels: the average position of #>   their sites.

text: wanang_butterflies holds butterfly counts 36 days three years. community differ years change months? Site variables (year month) taken data automatically, constant within day. Permutation tests whole model term: read . printout says year month together explain 23.6% variation butterfly composition (constrained fraction); rest variation among days variables account . constrained fraction 10-30% typical community data: species respond many things , counts rare species noisy. permutation test shuffles days many times refits model; p-value proportion shuffles explain much real data. terms significant : years differ composition, composition shifts steadily months (seasonality), independently year. title: Modelling diversity with tidymodels
text: model good predictions data seen. Cross-validation estimates honestly: split data folds, fit model one fold, predict held-fold, repeat. average prediction error (root mean squared error, RMSE, units response) measures well model generalises, comparing models shows whether extra variable genuinely helps fits noise. text: verbs give three dimensions. rarefaction extrapolation curves two Brazilian rainforest tree assemblages, using abundance data, phylogeny functional distances shipped iNEXT.3D.
code: library(ggplot2) data(list = c(   "Brazil_rainforest_abun_data", "Brazil_rainforest_phylo_tree",   "Brazil_rainforest_distance_matrix" ), package = "iNEXT.3D") wide <- Brazil_rainforest_abun_data brazil <- tibble(   site = rep(colnames(wide), each = nrow(wide)),   species = rep(rownames(wide), ncol(wide)),   n = unlist(wide, use.names = FALSE) ) |>   filter(n > 0)  curves <- bind_rows(   div_rarefy(brazil, abundance = n, type = "TD") |> mutate(type = "TD"),   div_rarefy(brazil,     abundance = n, type = "PD",     tree = Brazil_rainforest_phylo_tree   ),   div_rarefy(brazil,     abundance = n, type = "FD",     distance = as.matrix(Brazil_rainforest_distance_matrix)   ) )  curves$type <- factor(curves$type, levels = c("TD", "PD", "FD"))  ggplot(curves, aes(m, diversity, colour = site)) +   geom_line(aes(linetype = method == "extrapolation")) +   geom_point(data = filter(curves, method == "observed"), size = 2) +   facet_wrap(vars(q, type),     ncol = 3, scales = "free_y",     labeller = labeller(q = function(x) paste("q =", x), .multi_line = FALSE)   ) +   scale_linetype_manual(values = c("solid", "dashed"), guide = "none") +   labs(     x = "Number of individuals",     y = "Effective number of species", colour = NULL   ) +   theme_tidydiversity()

text: beta_mantel() tests whether two distance matrices correlated, example community dissimilarity elevational geographic distance, Mantel test (Mantel 1967). z, gives partial Mantel test x y controlling z (Smouse et al. 1986). Significance comes permuting sites x (vegan's vegan::mantel() vegan::mantel.partial()). Pairs sites independent, test distance-decay relationships ordinary regression p-values; use test instead. sites, use permutations = "exact" enumerate every ordering sites (n!; 5,040 7 sites); p-value exact. alternative sets tail: "greater" (default) tests positive correlation, "less" negative one (example similarity decreasing distance), "two.sided" either.

title: Mantel and partial Mantel tests — beta_mantel
code: beta_mantel(   x,   y,   z = NULL,   method = c("spearman", "pearson", "kendall"),   permutations = 9999,   alternative = c("greater", "less", "two.sided"),   strata = NULL,   seed = NULL )

title: Mantel and partial Mantel tests — beta_mantel
text: x, y, z Distance matrices: dist objects (result beta_dist()), square matrices, , y z, numeric vector site values (elevation), Euclidean distances computed. must describe sites order; carry labels, labels matched. method Correlation: "spearman" (default), "pearson" "kendall". permutations Number permutations, "exact". alternative "greater", "less" "two.sided". strata Optional grouping sites within permutations restricted. seed Optional random seed.

title: Mantel and partial Mantel tests — beta_mantel
text: one-row tibble statistic (Mantel r), p.value, alternative, permutations, exact, method partial.

title: Mantel and partial Mantel tests — beta_mantel
text: Mantel, N. (1967). detection disease clustering generalized regression approach. Cancer Research, 27, 209-220. Smouse, P. E., Long, J. C. Sokal, R. R. (1986). Multiple regression correlation extensions Mantel test matrix correspondence. Systematic Zoology, 35, 627-632.

title: Mantel and partial Mantel tests — beta_mantel

what: Partition beta diversity into turnover and nestedness — beta_pair
title: Partition beta diversity into turnover and nestedness — beta_pair
text: beta_pair() computes pairwise dissimilarity sites splits turnover (species replacement) nestedness (species loss) components following Baselga (2010, 2012). beta_multi() computes multiple-site version sites group. use presence absence, positive abundance counts presence. index = "sorensen" components Simpson turnover, nestedness-resultant component Sorensen dissimilarity. index = "jaccard" Jaccard equivalents. index = "bray" abundances used: turnover balanced variation abundance nestedness abundance gradient component Bray-Curtis dissimilarity (Baselga 2013), matching betapart::beta.pair.abund() betapart::beta.multi.abund().

title: Partition beta diversity into turnover and nestedness — beta_pair
code: beta_pair(   data,   site = site,   species = species,   abundance = NULL,   index = c("sorensen", "jaccard", "bray"),   .by = NULL )  beta_multi(   data,   site = site,   species = species,   abundance = NULL,   index = c("sorensen", "jaccard", "bray"),   .by = NULL )

title: Partition beta diversity into turnover and nestedness — beta_pair
text: data data frame long format, one row per record. site, species <tidy-select> column holding site identifiers column holding species names. abundance <tidy-select> column holding counts. NULL (default), column called abundance used present, otherwise every row counts one individual. index Family dissimilarity: "sorensen" "jaccard" (presence absence) "bray" (abundance-based Bray-Curtis). .<tidy-select> Optional grouping columns, kept output. Grouped data frames also respected.

title: Partition beta diversity into turnover and nestedness — beta_pair
text: beta_pair() returns tibble grouping columns, site_1, site_2, turnover, nestedness total. beta_multi() returns one row per group n_sites, turnover, nestedness total.

what: Shared species and similarity corrected for unseen species — beta_shared
title: Shared species and similarity corrected for unseen species — beta_shared
text: every pair sites: beta_shared() estimates total number species two sites share, including shared species neither sample detected, Chao1-shared estimator abundance data Chao2-shared estimator incidence data (Chao et al. 2000; Pan et al. 2009). beta_chao() gives abundance-based Jaccard Sørensen similarities Chao et al. (2005), correct shared species missed incomplete samples, next classic indices. Classic indices underestimate similarity samples incomplete, species shared two sites rare one often missed. Chao versions estimate probability individual one site belongs species shared (u, v), adding shared species seen one sample. estimators EstimateS SpadeR; values equal SpadeR's, chao_jaccard equals one minus vegan's vegdist(method = "chao"). checked test suite.

what: Biotic homogenisation between two surveys — div_homogenisation
title: Biotic homogenisation between two surveys — div_homogenisation
text: div_homogenisation() asks whether communities become alike time, widespread alien species spread local endemics lost (biotic homogenisation; McKinney Lockwood 1999; Olden Rooney 2006). computes mean pairwise similarity among sites two surveys (Jaccard Sorensen, presence-absence) change, \(\Delta = \bar S_{} - \bar S_{}\): positive values mean homogenisation, negative values differentiation. Site pairs share sites, independent. confidence interval therefore resamples sites (site bootstrap): sites drawn replacement, change recomputed pairs distinct drawn sites. status, change also computed native species : difference two (alien_contribution) part change due alien species.

Data: "abundances" #> • Zeros: "67%" — many zeros: shared absences must not make sites similar #>   (Hellinger or Bray-Curtis) #> • Species in one site only: "10%" #> • Gradient length (DCA axis 1, SD units): "3.52" — intermediate: linear or #>   unimodal methods both suit #> • Site variables (model terms): "0" #>  #> ── Recommended ── #>  #> Approach: Unconstrained (indirect) ordination #> You want to describe the main patterns of composition, not test their causes. #> Method: PCA on Hellinger-transformed data, or NMDS #> Gradient length 3.5 SD; NMDS on bray dissimilarity suits any data. #> ord_fit(data, abundance = abundance, method = "pca", transform = "hellinger") #> ord_fit(data, abundance = abundance, method = "nmds", distance = "bray") #> Interpret: Fit site variables afterwards (arrows, contours, centroids) #> Fitted variables are a post hoc interpretation of the axes; their permutation #> p-values are descriptive. #> autoplot(ord, surface = <numeric variable>) #> Check: Scree diagram (PCA, CA) or Shepard diagram and stress (NMDS) #> How many axes are worth reading, and how faithful the diagram is. #> autoplot(ord, type = "scree")   # or type = "shepard" #> Plots: Biplot with numeric variables as contours or symbol size, factors as #> centroids; scree or Shepard inset; stability ellipses #> Contours show non-linear change that an arrow hides; the inset shows how #> faithful the diagram is; ellipses show which sites are placed firmly. #> autoplot(ord, surface = <numeric>, colour = <factor>, inset = "scree")   # "shepard" for NMDS #> autoplot(ord, type = "gradient", path = <numeric>) #> autoplot(ord, type = "stability") #> Interpret: Plain-language explanation of the tables and the diagram #> Variation explained, tests, directions of variables, #> ── tidyvisor: which analysis? ────────────────────────────────────────────────── #> Question: explain #>  #> ── What the data show ── #>  #> • Sites: "20" #> • Species: "30" #> • Data: "abundances" #> • Zeros: "67%" — many zeros: shared absences must not make sites similar #>   (Hellinger or Bray-Curtis) #> • Species in one site only: "10%" #> • Gradient length (DCA axis 1, SD units): "3.52" — intermediate: linear or #>   unimodal methods both suit #> • Site variables (model terms): "7" — many terms for the sites: select #>   variables (forward selection) #>  #> ── Recommended ── #>  #> Approach: Constrained (direct, canonical) ordination #> You have a hypothesis that measured site variables explain composition. #> Method: RDA on Hellinger-transformed data (or db-RDA) #> Gradient length 3.5 SD. #> ord <- ord_fit(data, abundance = abundance, method = "rda", transform = "hellinger", formula = ~A1 + Moisture + Management) #> Select: Forward selection of variables #> Too many or collinear variables inflate the explained variation and make the #> test unreliable. #> ord_select(data, abundance = abundance, formula = ~A1 + Moisture + Management) #> Test: Permutation tests: the whole model, each axis and each term #> The F-test of a constrained ordination has no parametric distribution; #> permuting sites gives p-values. #> ord_test(ord, by = "model"); ord_test(ord, by = title: Explain and interpret an ordination, its tests and its diagram — ord_interpret
code: data("dune", "dune.env", package = "vegan") d <- community_long(cbind(site = rownames(dune), dune.env, dune),   cols = dplyr::all_of(names(dune)) ) o <- ord_fit(d,   abundance = abundance, method = "rda", transform = "hellinger",   formula = ~ A1 + Management ) ord_interpret(o, permutations = 199) #>  #> ── tidyvisor: what the results show ──────────────────────────────────────────── #>  #> ── Overview ── #>  #> • A redundancy analysis (RDA) of 20 sites and 30 species #>   (Hellinger-transformed), constrained by A1, Management. #>  #> ── Variation ── #>  #> • The site variables explain 38.6% of the variation in composition (adjusted R² #>   = 22.2%, allowing for the number of variables). #> • The first two constrained axes hold 17.5% and 13.2% of the total variation #>   (79.5% of the explained part). #>  #> ── Tests ── #>  #> • Overall, composition is significantly related to the site variables #>   (permutation F = 2.35, p = 0.005, 199 permutations). #> • A1 has no significant unique effect (F = 2.09, p = 0.065), after allowing for #>   the other variables. #> • Management has a significant unique effect (F = 2.08, p = 0.015), after #>   allowing for the other variables. #>  #> ── Site variables ── #>  #> • A1 increases towards the lower left of the diagram, mostly along the first #>   axis (biplot scores -0.65, -0.59). #> • Management: BF lies towards the upper right; HF lies towards the right; NM #>   lies towards the left; SF lies towards the lower right. The further apart two #>   centroids, the more the composition of their sites differs. #>  #> ── Species ── #>  #> • Axis 1 (RDA1) runs from Eleopalu, Ranuflam, Comapalu (negative end) to #>   Poatriv, Lolipere, Poaprat (positive end). #> • Axis 2 (RDA2) runs from Agrostol, Alopgeni, Poatriv (negative end) to #>   Planlanc, Anthodor, Scorautu (positive end). #>  #> ── Reading the diagram ── #>  #> • Sites (circles) close together have similar species composition. #> • With species scaling, the angles between species (and between species and #>   variable arrows) approximate their correlations; distances between sites are #>   only approximate. #> • Project a site or species perpendicularly onto an arrow: the further along #>   the arrow, the higher the variable (or the stronger the species' association #>   with it). #> • Triangles are the centroids of the factor levels: the average position of #>   their sites.

title: Principal response curves — ord_prc
text: ord_prc() fits principal response curves (PRC; van den Brink ter Braak 1999), partial redundancy analysis shows community treatment departs control time, time condition. treatment's departure time one canonical coefficient, species weight: species large positive weights follow curves, species large negative weights opposite. autoplot() draws classic PRC diagram: curves treatments time, control zero line, species weights scale beside .

title: Principal response curves — ord_prc
code: # Chlorpyrifos in experimental ditches (van den Brink and ter Braak 1999): # 12 ditches, 11 sampling weeks, five doses; abundances already log-transformed data("pyrifos", package = "vegan") ditch <- gl(12, 1, length = 132) week <- gl(11, 12, labels = c(-4, -1, 0.1, 1, 2, 4, 8, 12, 15, 19, 24)) dose <- factor(rep(c(0.1, 0, 0, 0.9, 0, 44, 6, 0.1, 44, 0.9, 0, 6), 11)) pyr <- data.frame(site = paste(ditch, week, sep = "_"), dose, week, pyrifos) pyr <- community_long(pyr, cols = dplyr::all_of(names(pyrifos))) p <- ord_prc(pyr,   treatment = dose, time = week, abundance = abundance,   transform = "none", permutations = 99 ) p #> Principal response curves: 4 treatments against "0", 11 times. #> Treatment explains 42.8% of the variation after time; first axis F = 15.1, p = #> 0.01. ggplot2::autoplot(p, weights = 1)

what: Mid-domain null model of richness along a gradient — range_mde
title: Mid-domain null model of richness along a gradient — range_mde
text: species' ranges placed random within bounded gradient, overlap middle, richness peaks mid-gradient even environmental cause: mid-domain effect (Colwell Hurtt 1994; Colwell Lees 2000). range_mde() builds null model observed ranges, spirit RangeModel (Colwell 2008), compares observed richness site. species keeps observed range size (number consecutive sampled sites spans, range_through() interpolation), position randomised: model = "uniform": every position range fits equally likely (Colwell Hurtt 1994). expected richness computed exactly; interval comes nsim randomisations. model = "spread": range starts random site spreads random neighbouring sites ("spreading dye" model Jetz Rahbek 2001, rangemodelR package), places ranges near ends uniform model. Sites treated positions order along gradient, model assumes sampled sites represent domain evenly.

what: Geometry or environment? Partitioning richness along a gradient — range_partition
title: Geometry or environment? Partitioning richness along a gradient — range_partition
text: range_partition() splits variation observed richness along gradient part explained mid-domain null model (geometry), part explained environmental variables, part share, unexplained rest. variation partitioning (Borcard et al. 1992; Peres-Neto et al. 2006) adjusted R², applied debate whether geometric constraints environment drive richness gradients (Colwell et al. 2004; Dunn et al. 2007). Unique fractions tested F test nested linear models. sites (single-mountain transects) tests little power adjusted fractions can negative (read negative values zero); report descriptive. Sites along gradient also spatially autocorrelated, makes p-values small.

title: Range shifts between two surveys of the same gradient — range_shift_resurvey
text: range_shift_resurvey() compares species' ranges historical survey resurvey gradient (example elevational transect decades apart; Moritz et al. 2008; Freeman Freeman 2014). species found surveys gives shift lower edge, upper edge, midpoint abundance-weighted optimum, change breadth; species found one survey listed "lost" "new". range_shift_test() asks whether species shifted average. Species share gradient survey design, shifts treated units replication, published resurveys: gives mean shift measure, bootstrap confidence interval resampling species, exact two-sided sign test whether species moved . Shifts edges end sampled gradient unreliable, default edges flagged truncated either survey left test edge.

what: Validate projected range shifts against resurveys (hindcasting) — range_shift_validate
title: Validate projected range shifts against resurveys (hindcasting) — range_shift_validate
text: range-shift model earns trust predicts shifts already happened. range_shift_validate() compares shifts observed historical survey resurvey (range_shift_resurvey()) shifts model predicted species period, run climate first survey second (hindcasting). measure (lower edge, upper edge, midpoint, optimum) reports: bias: mean predicted minus observed shift (m); mae, rmse: mean absolute root mean square error (m); r, rho: Pearson Spearman correlation across species; slope: calibration slope observed predicted (1 ideal; 1, model overstates differences species); direction: share species whose shift predicted sign; tracking: mean observed shift divided mean predicted shift, share expected shift species realised (1 = full tracking; 1, lag), bootstrap interval resampling species. range_shift_expected() gives simplest prediction, isotherm shift \(\Delta T / \gamma\) warming \(\Delta T\) lapse rate \(\gamma\) (Colwell et al. 2008; Freeman Freeman 2014). baseline model must beat.

what: ForestGEO-style stem and tree census verbs — stems
title: ForestGEO-style stem and tree census verbs — stems
text: Tidyverse-style helpers ForestGEO / CTFS plot inventories. accept data frames usual columns (plot, census, treeID, stemID, gx, gy, dbh, species / sp, status, optionally date) return tibbles. Callers stay inside tidydiversity instead using fgeo CTFS packages. Typical workflow: standardise names stems_as_trees() (main stem per tree) keep stems; summarise stems_abundance() stems_basal_area(); size classes stems_size_class(); demography two censuses stems_demography(); feed species counts div_hill() via stems_as_community(). Spatial stem verbs (quadrats, habitat joins, neighbourhoods, torus-translation habitat test) stem maps topography companion package tidymapr (tidymapr::stems_quadrat(), tidymapr::stems_habitat_test(), tidymapr::plot_topo()). Basal area one stem \eqn{\pi/4 \times \mathrm{dbh}^2} (Condit 1998; fgeo.analyze). dbh_unit = "cm" result cm\(^2\); "mm" mm\(^2\). Convert afterwards need m\(^2\) ha\(^{-1}\).

code: data("dune", "dune.env", package = "vegan") d <- community_long(cbind(site = rownames(dune), dune.env, dune),   cols = dplyr::all_of(names(dune)) ) # Before: which analysis? tidyvisor(d, abundance = abundance, formula = ~ A1 + Management) #>  #> ── tidyvisor: which analysis? ────────────────────────────────────────────────── #> Question: explain #>  #> ── What the data show ── #>  #> • Sites: "20" #> • Species: "30" #> • Data: "abundances" #> • Zeros: "67%" — many zeros: shared absences must not make sites similar #>   (Hellinger or Bray-Curtis) #> • Species in one site only: "10%" #> • Gradient length (DCA axis 1, SD units): "3.52" — intermediate: linear or #>   unimodal methods both suit #> • Site variables (model terms): "4" #>  #> ── Recommended ── #>  #> Approach: Constrained (direct, canonical) ordination #> You have a hypothesis that measured site variables explain composition. #> Method: RDA on Hellinger-transformed data (or db-RDA) #> Gradient length 3.5 SD. #> ord <- ord_fit(data, abundance = abundance, method = "rda", transform = "hellinger", formula = ~A1 + Management) #> Test: Permutation tests: the whole model, each axis and each term #> The F-test of a constrained ordination has no parametric distribution; #> permuting sites gives p-values. #> ord_test(ord, by = "model"); ord_test(ord, by = "axis"); ord_test(ord, by = "margin") #> Plots: Triplot; species response curves along the main variable; t-value biplot #> or Van Dobben circles #> The triplot shows sites, species and variables together; response curves show #> each species' optimum and tolerance with confidence bands; Van Dobben circles #> single out the species that respond significantly. #> autoplot(ord) #> autoplot(ord, type = "response", variable = "<numeric>") #> autoplot(ord, type = "vandobben", variable = "<numeric>") #> Interpret: Plain-language explanation of the tables and the diagram #> Variation explained, tests, directions of variables, groups, species at each #> end of the axes, and how to read the plot. #> ord_interpret(ord) # After: what does it show? o <- ord_fit(d,   abundance = abundance, method = "rda", transform = "hellinger",   formula = ~ A1 + Management ) tidyvisor(o, permutations = 199) #>  #> ── tidyvisor: what the results show ──────────────────────────────────────────── #>  #> ── Overview ── #>  #> • A redundancy analysis (RDA) of 20 sites and 30 species #>   (Hellinger-transformed), constrained by A1, Management. #>  #> ── Variation ── #>  #> • The site variables explain 38.6% of the variation in composition (adjusted R² #>   = 22.2%, allowing for the number of variables). #> • The first two constrained axes hold 17.5% and 13.2% of the total variation #>   (79.5% of the explained part). #>  #> ── Tests ── #>  #> • Overall, composition is significantly related to the site variables #>   (permutation F = 2.35, p = 0.005, 199 permutations). #> • A1 has a significant unique effect (F = 2.09, p = 0.045), after allowing for #>   the other variables. #> • Management has a significant unique effect (F = 2.08, p = 0.015), after #>   allowing for the other variables. #>  #> ── Site variables ── #>  #> • A1 increases towards the lower left of the diagram, mostly along the first #>   axis (biplot scores -0.65, -0.59). #> • Management: BF lies towards the upper right; HF lies towards the right; NM #>   lies towards the left; SF lies towards the lower right. The further apart two #>   centroids, the more the composition of their sites differs. #>  #> ── Species ── #>  #> • Axis 1 (RDA1) runs from Eleopalu, Ranuflam, Comapalu (negative end) to #>   Poatriv, Lolipere, Poaprat (positive end). #> • Axis 2 (RDA2) runs from Agrostol, Alopgeni, Poatriv (negative end) to #>   Planlanc, Anthodor, Scorautu (positive end). #>  #> ── Reading the diagram ── #>  #> • Sites (circles) close together have similar species composition. #> • With species scaling, the angles between species (and between species and #>   variable arrows) approximate their correlations; distances between sites are #>   only approximate. #> • Project a site or species perpendicularly onto an arrow: the further along #>   the arrow, the higher the variable (or the stronger the species' association #>   with it). #> • Triangles are the centroids of the factor levels: the average position of #>   their sites.

title: Standardised effect sizes from null models — trait_ses
text: Null models: "traits": shuffle trait values among species (keeps every site's species richness abundances; tests trait structure). "richness": shuffle abundances among species within site (keeps richness abundance distribution site). "swap": independent swap site x species matrix, keeping site species totals (vegan::nullmodel(), "quasiswap_count").

title: Functional diversity from trait probability densities — trait_tpd
text: trait probability density (TPD) approach (Carmona et al. 2016, 2019) describes species probability density trait values, estimated individual measurements, intraspecific variability part every index. Community TPDs abundance-weighted sums species TPDs. , trait_tpd() returns functional richness, evenness divergence (TPD::REND()) functional redundancy (TPD::redundancy()) per site, trait_tpd_dissim() returns pairwise functional dissimilarity sites, split shared non-shared parts (TPD::dissim()).
